column10: Figure 39-1 Multi-channel schema for LAION-5B image-text candidate records
column15: Multi-channel schema for LAION-5B image-text candidate records. Source: original illustration based on the LAION-5B paper and LAION dataset-spec.
column16:
This figure explains that a LAION-5B image-text sample should be understood as a governable candidate record rather than a simple pair of one
  image and one caption. The center of the diagram is a stable candidate record with fields such as uid, image_url, text, clip_score, nsfw_score,
  watermark_score, shard_id, and removal_status. Around this record are five information channels. The web trace channel records the Common Crawl
  WAT source, image URL, alt text, and page URL. The text channel records language, text hash, and caption-noise information. The visual channel
  records download status, image width and height, and image hash. The alignment channel records the CLIP model, CLIP score, and filtering
  threshold, while emphasizing that CLIP score only measures image-text relevance and is not full quality assurance. The risk channel records NSFW,
  watermark, face-privacy, and license-hint signals. The release channel records dataset version, shard identifier, and removal status. On the
  right side, the same stable record is shown feeding different task views: a training-view preview, an evaluation-view preview, and a governance-
  view preview. A caption example below the record shows how a text caption may appear in one view while other metadata supports filtering,
  auditing, removal, and release governance. The legend distinguishes stable data links, non-channel notes or hints, and variable task views.

column3: Part 12: Specialized Datasets and Multimodal Data Engineering Practice
column5: Chapter 39: Image-Text Data Engineering: Candidate Pool Construction, Multimodal Filtering, and DataComp Evaluation
column9: Figure 39-2 Image-text candidate-pool quality evaluation and closed-loop repair
column10: Figure 39-2 Image-text candidate-pool quality evaluation and closed-loop repair
column15: Image-text candidate-pool quality evaluation and closed-loop repair. Source: original illustration based on the LAION-5B paper and DataComp benchmark design.
column16:
This figure describes a closed-loop quality evaluation and repair workflow for an image-text candidate pool. The process starts with candidate
  metadata, including URL, text, and quality scores. It then applies five-channel quality checks: the text channel checks caption noise and
  language confidence; the visual channel checks download success, image size, and image hash; the alignment channel checks CLIP score and human
  pass rate; the risk channel checks NSFW content, watermark, face privacy, and related safety risks; and the release channel checks manifest
  coverage, URL status, and the removal ledger.

  Samples that fail or raise uncertainty are routed into a risk queue. The queue includes URL decay, caption noise, watermark or copyright issues,
  NSFW content and minors, faces and privacy, and possible evaluation contamination. Repair actions include redownloading, refiltering,
  downweighting, quarantining, or removing problematic samples. After repair, approved data is written into a frozen training view, including the
  manifest, shards, and sample seed, so that experiments can be reproduced.

  The final stage evaluates candidate-pool filters under a fixed DataComp-style protocol: the model, hyperparameters, and benchmarks remain fixed,
  and only the data filtering strategy g changes. The formula S(g) represents a weighted benchmark score used to compare different filtering
  strategies. The main message is that image-text data quality should not rely on post-training fallback; quality should be controlled through
  channel checks, risk handling, repair actions, and reproducible evaluation before training.

column15: Four-stage SparseTable-Bench construction pipeline.
column16: The diagram presents the four-stage construction pipeline for SparseTable-Bench. Stage one collects table images from scientific papers, financial reports, and clinical-trial documents. The collection includes borderless tables, whitespace-based layouts, empty columns, and complex headers, while preserving source and dataset-split information. Stage two extracts a parseable HTML tree, preserves merged-row and merged-column relationships, and explicitly represents empty cells. Stage three assigns a spatial boundary to every cell, including blank cells, and checks row alignment, column alignment, and boundary validity. Stage four creates sparse-topology stress samples through column-aware masking. Text may be removed, but the row and column structure must remain intact. Consistency checks throughout the pipeline ensure that the HTML is parseable, cell order is preserved, spatial boundaries are valid, and dataset versions and splits remain aligned.

column10: Figure 40-6: STB-Mask-Stress occlusion generation and evaluation workflow
column15: The occlusion strategy of STB-Mask-Stress is column-aware. The workflow can be summarized as follows. 1. Parse the original table structure to obtain the row-column index, header/body membership, and bounding box of each cell. 2. Randomly select a subset of columns as occlusion candidates.
column16: The diagram shows the STB-Mask-Stress sample-generation and evaluation workflow. First, the original table is parsed to obtain its HTML grid, rows, columns, and cell boundaries. Second, one or two candidate columns are selected randomly. Third, one of three masking modes is chosen: body masking, header masking, or random sparse masking. Fourth, the corresponding image regions are covered with a uniform background. Fifth, the annotations are updated by removing or resetting the masked text while preserving the table structure. Sixth, the generated samples are evaluated for structural similarity, empty-position recall, and different categories of error. Body masking preserves the header while hiding body columns. Header masking hides the header while preserving the body. Random sparse masking hides selected body cells to simulate scanning damage, occlusion, or local sparsity. The central principle is that textual evidence may be hidden, but structural nodes, empty cells, spatial alignment, and table topology must remain intact.

column16:
This figure presents the MedImage-ToolVQA dataset construction flow as a left-to-right pipeline. The
  process begins with region-level samples, which contain a medical image, a region of interest, mask or bounding box, and a
  target description. These samples are converted into multiple-choice visual question answering examples during question
  generation. At this stage, the question must depend on the image and must not leak the bounding-box coordinates directly. The
  next stage performs quality verification, checking that the schema is complete, the answer is consistent, and the question is
  locally grounded in visual evidence. Verified examples then produce tool observations, such as zoomed crops, mask overlays, or
  segmentation images. These observations are used to synthesize trajectories that include reasoning fragments, tool calls, and
  explicit use of the returned observation. The final stage packages the result into training data, including SFT dialogues,
  reinforcement-learning environment inputs, and reward fields. A summary band at the bottom emphasizes two constraints: every
  question must trace back to a reviewable local image region, and every tool action must explain which visual uncertainty it
  resolves.

column9: Figure 41-7: Multi-turn structure of tool-call trajectories
column10: Figure 41-7: Multi-turn structure of tool-call trajectories
column15: Multi-turn structure of a tool-call trajectory. Tool observations return as new image inputs; the model must continue reasoning from the observation image rather than merely produce a formally correct call.
column16:
This figure explains the structure of a multi-turn tool-call trajectory for medical image question
  answering. The sequence has four main steps connected from left to right. First, the task input comes from the user message and
  includes the original medical image, the question with candidate answer options, and metadata such as image index, image size,
  and region cues. Second, the assistant makes a decision action: it judges whether the whole-image evidence is sufficient,
  chooses whether to zoom in, run segmentation, or answer directly, and emits a valid tool name with JSON arguments when a tool
  is needed. Third, the tool or user message returns an observation, such as a crop, mask overlay, or segmentation result. This
  returned observation is inserted into the next dialogue turn while preserving the source region and tool arguments. Fourth, the
  assistant consumes the new observation, updates its judgment, calls tools again only if evidence is still insufficient, and
  finally outputs the selected option with a brief reason. A loop arrow shows that insufficient evidence sends the process back
  to the decision step. The core constraint is that tool-returned observations become part of the next context turn and remain
  traceable to the final answer.

column15: Latent-Switch-69K distills reasoning traces from Dolci-Think-SFT-32B into solution intuitions, compressed CoT, latent budgets, student sequences, and mask-aligned SFT records.
column16: The figure presents a left-to-right data engineering pipeline for building Latent-Switch-69K. Source reasoning traces from Dolci-Think-SFT-32B are first extracted and normalized. A teacher model then distills each long reasoning trace into two complementary components: a high-level solution intuition and a compressed explicit chain-of-thought. The solution intuition is used to estimate the number of latent reasoning slots, while the compressed chain-of-thought and final answer remain visible in the student sequence. The rendered training record contains a latent reasoning interval, an explicit reasoning interval, and an answer span. The final stage constructs supervision masks so that prompt tokens and latent interior placeholders are ignored by ordinary cross-entropy, while structural boundaries, explicit reasoning, answer tokens, and selected teacher-KL positions receive targeted supervision. The purpose of the figure is to show that reasoning-trace compression is not simple summarization; it is a structured transformation from long visible reasoning into an auditable training record with hidden planning budget, visible verification, and mask-controlled objectives.

column15: The extensive visible reasoning in the source trace is split into two types of signal: solution intuition is used to estimate the latent budget, and the compressed CoT is used for explicit verification and answer supervision.
column16: The figure contrasts three representations of reasoning data. The original representation contains a long visible chain-of-thought, where most of the token budget is spent on detailed intermediate reasoning. The compressed representation separates the high-level solution plan from the explicit verification path: the solution intuition captures planning information, and the compressed chain-of-thought retains only the visible reasoning needed to justify the answer. The latent-switch representation then maps the solution intuition into a bounded number of latent placeholders, followed by a shorter visible chain-of-thought and the final answer.

column10: Figure 43-4: Distributions of Original and Distilled Reasoning Length and Compression Ratio
column15: This figure shows the distributions of source CoT length, distilled CoT length, intuition length, ground truth length, and compression ratio.
column16: The figure visualizes corpus-level distributions used to audit the compression process in Latent-Switch-69K. It compares the length of the original reasoning trace with the length of the distilled explicit chain-of-thought, the length of the solution intuition, the length of the ground-truth or final answer, and the resulting compression ratio. The compression ratio is defined as distilled chain-of-thought length divided by original chain-of-thought length. The chapter reports a mean compression ratio of 0.612 and a median of 0.569, indicating that the visible reasoning trace is substantially shortened but not reduced to only the answer. The purpose of the figure is to support quality control: compressed samples should reduce token cost while preserving enough explicit verification to connect the question to the final answer. Extremely short compressed traces may indicate over-compression, while unusually long traces may indicate insufficient compression or unstable distillation.

column15: Prompt and latent interior tokens are masked from ordinary CE; latent boundaries, explicit CoT, answers, and end tokens are controlled by different weights and masks.
column16: The figure shows how different parts of a latent-switch training sequence receive different supervision. The prompt and assistant prefix serve as conditioning context and are assigned ignored labels for ordinary cross-entropy. The latent interval begins with a supervised <latent_think> boundary token, contains latent interior placeholders that are masked from ordinary cross-entropy, and ends with a supervised </latent_think> boundary token. The visible reasoning interval, enclosed by <think> and </think>, is supervised as compressed explicit reasoning and may receive a reduced chain-of-thought loss weight. The final answer span receives strong answer supervision because it is the primary location of task correctness. Teacher-KL supervision applies only to selected explicit reasoning and answer positions, not to the latent interior placeholders. The figure emphasizes that masks are part of the data schema: changing token boundaries, tokenizer behavior, or sequence rendering can change the training objective.

This diagram shows how text-to-video training data is processed from video sources into a trainable dataset. Public videos, CC0 asset libraries, and self-collected data are first segmented into single-shot clips, then filtered through motion detection to remove blurred, jittery, watermarked, or low-quality samples. Multi-frame captioning, spatiotemporal alignment, and cinematic language annotation produce structured textual information. The data is then stratified by resolution, quality tier, and SFT requirements, forming a trainable T2V dataset with manifests and audit logs.

Data is first screened for hard-blocking risks such as adult content, CSAM, PII, and illegal samples, then reviewed for copyright risk, license status, opt-out lists, logos, watermarks, and brand marks. The system further checks OCR text, subtitle occlusion, borders, low resolution, blur, and compression noise, before routing samples by aesthetics, PickScore, HPSv2, motion, diversity, and rare concepts. When these signals are further reinforced by online traffic feedback, the trained model may gradually move away from the real data distribution, leading to late-stage performance degradation or model collapse. The mechanism highlights the need for continuous monitoring and feedback isolation when using synthetic data.

Validated data enters gray-scale release and online monitoring, where a canary release gate checks production risk. When anomalies are detected, the system triggers risk alerts, version freezes, rollbacks, template revision, real-data back-injection, and reduction of the synthetic data proportion.
